answer.rationale:
Timeline is the strongest signal available: a release landed 2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90m ago, so the release is the leading suspect and rollback is the only candidate that addresses a cause rather than a symptom. memory_b2 explicitly forbids regional_failover while writes are hot (40-minute replication gap, two accounts lost writes) and settlement writes are at daily peak, so failover is disqualified against the objective of not losing customer writes. add_capacity (memory_b3) helps queue-depth saturation ahead of a known surge, not a regression that started mid-day; route_read_replicas (memory_b5) relieves read pressure on the primary and would not fix a write-path regression introduced by a deploy; enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contains a failing downstream dependency, and nothing here points to a partner failure. I want memory_b1 verified because I am leaning on it hardest and its summary is suspiciously clean: I need the original record to know whether that rollback was executed under heavy write load and whether the prior build was schema-compatible, since a rollback across a migration during peak settlement is exactly how writes get lost. I want memory_b6 verified because canary cohorts caught prior bad builds within an hour; if this release also had canary gating, the original record tells me whether cohort-level signal exists that would either confirm the release as cause or exonerate it. Correlation is not causation here \\\
dash the latency climb could predate the deploy's traffic ramp or track the settlement peak itself, so I am scoping this as a guarded partial rollback on a limited cohort with write-integrity monitoring and a migration-compatibility check before any fleet-wide reversal, holding the other levers for the next window.
